records.name: Blue Action Fund
records.summary: Grant-based fund that supports marine conservation projects implemented by NGOs and other partners to conserve the ocean and improve the livelihoods of coastal communities in developing countries in Africa, Latin America and Asia/Pacific. Primary focus is on Marine protected Areas and OECMs. Funding is through Calls for Proposals, usually issued once a year, with a 25% match-funding requirement.
records.intermediaries: IUCN, KfW, Nature Trust Alliance, German Committee of the UN- Ocean Decade 2021-2031, Hogan Lovells
records.implementers: international and national NGOs (excluding intergovernmental organisations), third party/organisations (including not-for-profit organisations and  commercial companies).  Active grants in Cambodia include a project implemented by non profit organizations like Fauna and Flora, with Song Saa Foundation, Children and Women’s Development Center in Cambodia, Fisheries Action Coalition Team, Fishing Cat Ecological Enterprise as partners.
records.capital: Public. Core funders include the KfW Development Bank,  the Agence Française de Développement (AFD), the Norwegian Agency for Development Cooperation (Norad), and Irish Aid. Other funders include GCF and the Swedish Ministry for Foreign Affairs.
records.scale: Landscape/seascape (site-specific, for MPAs and OECMs, individually or in networks, national or transboundary)
records.thematic: Marine protected area governance, sustainable livelihoods, species conservation, sustainable fisheries, habitat conservation and restoration, equitable decision-making and community empowerment, climate adaptation, gender equity
records.size: Funding  is usually between EUR 2 - 4 million, in exceptional cases up to EUR 5 million; and for a duration of three to five years.
records.frequency: Usually once a year since 2016, however no funding calls were issued in 2025 or so far in 2026.
records.targetGroups: Local coastal communities, NGOs and Marine Protected Area administrations · local communities, NGOs, women
records.activities: Examples include reduction of harvest losses in fisheries, gear selectivity, co-management initatives,  habitat restoration for mangroves, coral reefs, seagrass beds, staff training, etc.
records.whoCanApply: The funding process involves applications to advertised Calls for Proposals. Grantees and sub-grantees are usually NGOs or other non-profit organizations that are able to fund at least 25% of the total project costs through their own resources and funding from other donors.
records.enablingEnv:
Relevant policies and standards applicable:
All project activities need to be compliant with the legal framework of the project host country(ies), while adhering to the requirements of the international good practice standards. This is based on the Blue Action Fund Environmental and Social Management System, which is underpinned by a number of international Environmental and Social Standards and Guidelines, such as:
- The World Bank Environmental and Social Framework (ESF)
- ILO Core Labour Standards
- KfW Sustainability Guideline - Assessment of Environmental, Social, and Climate Performance: Principles and Process (including KfW Bankengruppe’s Declaration on the Consideration of Human Rights in its Business Operations)
- The World Bank Group’s Environmental, Health and Safety (EHS) Guidelines, including General EHS Guidelines and Industry Specific Guidelines, as applicable.
- BMZ’s Guidelines on Incorporating Human Rights Standards and Principles, Including Gender, in Programme Proposals for Bilateral German Technical and Financial Cooperation
- “Workers’ Accommodation: Processes and Standards: A Guidance Note by IFC and the EBRD”
- FAO Voluntary Guidelines on the Responsible Governance of Tenure of Land, Fisheries and Forests in the Context of National Food Security (VGGT)
- FAO Code of Conduct for Responsible Fisheries
- FAO Voluntary Guidelines for Securing Sustainable Small-Scale Fisheries (VGSSF).
- UN Code of Conduct for Law Enforcement Officials
- Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials
- The Voluntary Principles on Security and Human Rights

records.name: Asian Development Bank (ADB) Natural Capital Fund (NCF)
records.summary: The NCF is a close-ended USD 150 million catalytic natural capital blended finance fund, designed and managed by ADB, that aims to support SMEs in ADB-member countries implementing agri-food systems projects that enhance food security and protect, restore, and sustainably use natural capital.
records.intermediaries: ADB and GEF
records.implementers: The fund often relies on local financial institutions to implement finance.
records.capital: Public and private (sovereign donors, development agencies, climate funds, philanthropies, and corporates)
records.instruments: Grants, debt, equity and guarantees · Grants, loans/debt, equity, guarantees
records.thematic: climate smart agri-food systems projects that protect, restore, and sustainably use natural capital
records.size: Funding may range between USD 200,000 and USD 10 million+, depending on the stage of the business and type of investment.
records.frequency: Project origination may occur through ADB country offices, govenrments, regional cooperation hubs, or through direct invitations to apply.
records.targetGroups: SMEs and smallholder farmers, specifically at the pre-seed, seed, and early stages · SMEs, smallholders
records.activities: Sustainable Agriculture & Food Systems: Initiatives for regenerative farming, agroforestry, and low-chemical farming to boost food security.
records.requirements: Investments (SMEs and/or intermediaries) must contribute to address the negative externalities and inefficiencies of the agri-food systems in which they operate and have a strong focus on protecting, restoring, and sustainably using natural capital.
records.whoCanApply: Funding is available directly to SMEs or indirectly via financial intermediaries (e.g. public investors [governments, national DFIs, state corporations, etc.,] and commercial investors [banks, asset managers (private debt and private equity), corporates, etc.]).

records.name: Adaptation Fund
records.summary: The Fund helps developing countries build resilience and adapt to climate change and gives them full ownership of adaptation projects, from planning through implementation, while ensuring monitoring and transparency.
records.intermediaries: World Bank
records.implementers: The Cambodian Environment Ministry is the Fund’s deisgnated authority in Cambodia, and often implements projects alongside Multilateral Implementing Entities like the UN Human Settlement Programme (UN-Habitat), UNIDO and UNEP. The Ministry is responsible for endorsing projects porposed by such entities.
records.capital: Public and private: Primarily financed through voluntary contributions from governments and private donors, plus a 2% share of proceeds from Certified Emission Reductions (CERs) from Kyoto Protocol Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) projects.
records.thematic: thematic focus areas include Agriculture, Food Security, Ecosystem-based adaptation, Forests and Rural development
records.size: Recent grants have been up to USD 10million for a duration of 2-3 years. The Adaptation Fund funds small-size projects and programmes (up to USD 1 million); and larger ("regular") projects and programmes (over USD 1 million).
records.frequency: Funding requests are accepted on a rolling basis; approvals are granted at Board meetings which occur 2x per year.
records.targetGroups:
Small-scale farmers
Local communities
Women's groups
Indigenous Peoples · smallholders, local communities, women
records.activities:
Ecosystem-based adaptation
Sustainable agriculture
Water management
Disaster risk reduction
Urban/rural development
records.requirements: The main criteria include legal status and ability to enter into a contract; existence of financial statements including Project Accounts statement and internal and external audits; internal control framework, especially with respect to disbursements and payments, and business plans, budgets and the ability to monitor expenditure. Other criteria include the ability to comply with the Fund's gender policy and environmental and social policy through all phases of the project cycle. These and other aspects of the application process are explained in the Fund's Operational Policies and Guidelines. See also the section on aspects of the required enabling environment.
records.whoCanApply: Funding is not directly accissible.
records.enablingEnv:
Underlying policies and standards applicable: The Environmental and Social Policy and Gender Guidance Document describe the major aspects of the required enabling environment. As part of the implementing entities’ responsibilities for the project/programme, all implementing entities shall (i) have an environmental and social management system that ensures environmental and social risks are identified and assessed at the earliest possible stage of project/programme design, (ii) adopt measures to avoid or where avoidance is impossible to minimize or mitigate those risks during implementation, and (iii) monitor and report on the status of those measures during and at the end of implementation.
All projects/programmes supported by the Fund have to be designed and implemented to meet the following environmental and social principles, as relevant:
- compliance with domestic and international law
- fair and equitable access to benefits
- avoid imposing any disproportionate adverse impacts on marginalized and vulnerable groups including children, women and girls, the elderly, indigenous people, tribal groups, displaced people, refugees, people living with disabilities, and people living with HIV/AIDS
- respect and promote international human rights
- promote gender equality and women's empowerment
- meet the core ILO labour standards-
- be consistent with the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples and other applicable international instruments relating to indigenous peoples
- avoid or minimize the need for involuntary resettlement
-  shall not involve unjustified conversion or degradation of critical natural habitats, reduction or loss of biological diversity or the introduction of known invasive species, or increase in greenhouse gas emissions or other climate change drivers
- prevent pollution and promote resource efficiency
- avoid public health impacts
- protect physical and cultural heritage.

records.name: Alterfin
records.summary: Alterfin is a Belgian social co-operative that offers investment opportunities to generate a positive social, environmental and economic impact. Since 1994, Alterfin has been financing social enterprises in Latin-America, Africa and Asia that support farmers and entrepreneurs in generating sustainable incomes.
records.intermediaries: None.
records.implementers: Alterfin works with target groups (local microfinance instititutions and sustainable smallholder agriculture organizations) directly. It has representatives based in Cambodia.
records.capital: Private. Co-operative members' investment through shares. Alterfin has over 5700 individuals and organizations as cooperative members.
records.thematic: Sustainable agriculture, climate change adaptation, poverty reduction, improving rural livelihoods, gender equality
records.size: Finance is provided between USD 100,000 and USD 1,500,000. For agricultral organizations, this can be in the form of short-term loans (3-12 months, for financing harvests) or long-term loans (up to five years to finance fixed assets).
records.frequency: rolling basis
records.targetGroups: sustainable smallholder agriculture organizations (including cooperatives and small and medium-sized agricultural enterprises) and microfinance institutions · SMEs, cooperatives, MFIs
records.activities:
Financial services: providing short- and long-term loans for microfinance institutions and agricultural SMEs to finance their working capital.
‍
Non-financial services: financing technical assistance projects
records.requirements:
The funding amount for short-term loans must be covered by sales contracts exceeding the value of the loan. For a long-term investment loan, the financed property is pledged as a guarantee.

Alterfin will not finance any organization on its exclusion list.

Eligibility criteria for sustainable smallholder agriculture organizations:

Years in operation: at least two years.
Ethos: clearly aligned with Alterfin’s key areas of focus: working primarily with smallholder farmers (no more than five hectares of land), clear environmental and/or social objectives, aiming to improve the living conditions of smallholder farmers, commitment to sustainable agriculture through fair trade, organic farming, etc.
Number of smallholder farmer beneficiaries: at least 150.
Annual sales: at least USD 500,000.
Operational self-sufficiency is > 90% and has a positive trend.

Eligibility criteria for microfinance institutions:

Years in operation: at least two years.
Minimum portfolio: USD 1,000,000.
Clientele: at least 1,000 clients or members.
Objectives: The MFI’s ethos and impact must be clearly aligned with Alterfin’s key areas of focus: fighting poverty, improving rural livelihoods, gender equality, and sustainable smallholder agriculture.
PAR 30 days + restructured loans + written-off loans < 10%.
Operational self-sufficiency > 80% and a positive trend.
Debt-to-equity ratio < = 5.

The financing process includes online submission of the application, shortlisting, due diligence and field visit, approval by the investment committee, contract and disbursement and follow-up.
records.whoCanApply: The loans can be accessed by co-operatives and small- and medium-sized agricultural enterprises, and other smallholder organizations, besides microfinance institutions.
records.enablingEnv:
Applicants: The eligibility criteria and loan disbursal process suggest that applicant organizations must have the legal capacity to enter into contracts and borrow funds.

Standards applicable to institutions involved: Alterfin has a tailored tool to assess partners’ social and environmental performance.
records.notes: Application to be sent to asia@alterfin.be.

records.name: GEF Small Grants Programme (SGP)
records.summary: The objective of the Small Grants Programme (SGP) is to mobilize civil society actors to address major drivers of environmental degradation while promoting sustainable development and improved livelihoods. The SGP operates in 135+ developing countries with a focus on LDCs and SIDS.
records.intermediaries: In the process of providing grant facilities, GEF SGP  cooperates with FAO, Conservation International and UNDP.
records.implementers: Typically local NGOs. For the 8th Operational Phase of the SGP, UNDP Cambodia is the implementing agency in Cambodia.
records.capital: Public. GEF-8 is funded by 29 donor governments, including Japan, Canada, Switzerland, Finland, Italy, Norway, New Zealand, and the USA. Since its inception GEF has been funded by a total of 40 donor countries.
records.thematic: Natural resource management, climate change adaptation, environmental sustainability, and community livelihoods.
records.size:
The program funds grants of up to USD 75,000. SGP also provides a maximum of USD 150,000 for strategic projects. These larger projects allow for scaling up and replication of successful approaches, covering a large number of communities within critical landscapes or seascapes.

Grantees have to match SGP funding with equivalent contribution from their own sources of funding (material, financial or in-kind) through local authority contribution and/or other donor support.
records.frequency: SGP publishes regular proposal calls.
records.targetGroups:
Rural populations
Indigenous Peoples
Women
Youth · local communities, IPLC, women, youth
records.activities:
Activities must be aligned with OP8 strategic priorities, or ICCA GSI phase 2 (Global Support Initiative for territories and areas conserved by Indigenous Peoples and local communities) or STAR-LD (System for Transparent Allocation of Resources for Land Degradation):

OP8 strategic priorities include:
1. Community-Based Biodiversity Conservation
- Conservation of endangered species through local stewardship
- Support for Indigenous and local communities to protect critical habitats
- Restoration of degraded ecosystems

2. Climate-Resilient Agriculture and Food Systems
- Promotion of agroecology and Climate-Smart Agriculture (CSA)
- Diversification of crops and livelihoods
- Water-efficient irrigation and soil conservation techniques

3. Sustainable Forest and Land Management
- Community Forestry, Community Protected Area and agroforestry models
- Prevention of illegal logging and land conversion
- Land tenure security and participatory land-use planning

4. Watershed and Wetland Restoration
- Rehabilitation of riparian zones and floodplains
- Community-led water monitoring and pollution control
- Integrated watershed governance

5. Renewable Energy and Energy Efficiency
- Deployment of solar, biogas, and clean cookstoves
- Energy access for off-grid communities
- Training in energy-efficient technologies

6. Waste Management and Circular Economy
- Community recycling and composting initiatives
- Reduction of plastic and hazardous waste
- Green enterprise development around waste reuse

7. Eco-Tourism and Cultural Heritage Protection
- Community-based tourism linked to conservation
- Preservation of cultural landscapes and sacred sites
- Training in sustainable tourism practices

8. Youth and Women Empowerment in Environmental Action
- Leadership training for women and youth
- Gender-responsive project design
- Inclusion of marginalized groups in decision-making

9. Environmental Education and Knowledge Sharing
- School-based environmental curricula
- Community awareness campaigns
- Local knowledge documentation and dissemination

10. Multi-Stakeholder Landscape Governance
- Platforms for CSO-government-private sector dialogue
- Participatory planning and co-management of resources
- Strengthening capacity of local institutions including local NGOs/CBOs, IPs organizations and community and policy advocacy

ICCAs Phase II proposes the following interventions:
1. Support legal recognition of ICCAs through policy advocacy, legal analysis, and engagement with government bodies.
2. Strengthen community capacity in conservation planning, climate resilience, and financial management via tailored training and mentorship.
3. Develop a national ICCAs registry and knowledge platform to consolidate data, showcase best practices, and support replication.
4. Promote inclusive governance by integrating gender and youth leadership modules into all ICCAs- supported activities.

From 2025 to 2028, OP8 Country STAR funding will focus on addressing land degradation.

Specifically, strategic grants are designed to:
i) Address systemic environmental challenges at a broader scale;
ii) Demonstrate replicable and scalable solutions that align with national priorities and GEF focal areas (e.g., biodiversity, climate change, land degradation);
iii) Engage multiple stakeholders, including government, civil society, and private sector actors; and
iv) Influence policy or institutional frameworks through evidence-based results.
records.requirements:
Applicants must be a registered local NGO, Community-Based Organizations,, Indigenous Peoples, Women and Youth group, or academic institution. Eligible organizations must operate in villages, communes, districts, and provinces within the Stung Siem Reap Watershed landscape in Siem Reap Province, in other biodiversity hotspots (see criteria below) across Cambodia, in areas with a high concentration of Indigenous Peoples, and nationwide under the STAR funding geographical areas. Applications may have to be submitted by post and must be prepared after engaging in scoping exercises led by UNDP GEF SGP team to assist in proposal development. The proposal format and other requirements are explained in the Guide to Access the GEF Small Grants Program.

The project proposal should include:
- Clear objectives aligned with OP8 strategic priorities, or ICCA GSI phase 2 or STAR-LD funding direction for funding.
- Description of the target Areas within the selected watershed or/and biodiversity hotspots or/and Areas with a High Concentration of Indigenous Peoples.
- Community engagement and gender/social inclusion plan
- Monitoring and evaluation framework

Key Criteria for Biodiversity Hotspots in Cambodia
i) Species Richness and Endemism
ii) Habitat Diversity
iii) Ecological Function and Connectivity
iv) Threat Level
v) Cultural and Socioeconomic Importance
vi) Legal and Institutional Recognition (Areas already designated as Protected Areas under Cambodia’s Ministry of Environment and sites recognized under international frameworks like the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) or ASEAN Heritage Parks)
records.whoCanApply: Local NGOs, Community-Based Organizations, and Indigenous Peoples’, Women and Youth groups, or academic institutions can apply directly for funding.
records.enablingEnv:
Underlying programmes, policies and conventions:
- According to the UNDP, the framework on STAR funding for Land Degradation provided by the Cambodian Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries supports the SGP in accelerating the implementation of Cambodia’s National Action Plan (NAP) on Land Degradation from 2025 to 2028.
- As mentioned in the eligibility requirements, for work proposed in biodiversity hotspots, areas should already be designated as Protected Areas under Cambodia’s Ministry of Environment and sites recognized under international frameworks like the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) or ASEAN Heritage Parks.
- The SGP is part of the GEF, which serves as a financial mechanism for several environmental conventions.

Applicants: must be legally registered entities.

Standards applicable to institutions involved:
The GEF policy on environmental and social safeguards outlines minimum standards for agency policies, including on:
- Environmental and Social Assessment, Management and Monitoring
- Accountability, Grievance and Conflict Resolution
- Biodiversity Conservation and the Sustainable Management of Living Natural Resources
- Restrictions on Land Use and Involuntary Resettlement
- Indigenous Peoples
- Cultural Heritage
- Resource Efficiency and Pollution Prevention
- Labour and Working Conditions
- Community Health, Safety and Security

records.name: Global Agriculture and Food Security Program (GAFSP)
records.summary: The Global Agriculture and Food Security Program (GAFSP) is a multilateral partnership and financing platform dedicated to improving food and nutrition security in the world’s poorest countries. It supports smallholder farmers, agribusinesses, and countries in the world’s poorest regions (focus on low-income countries), helping them withstand global shocks and build resilient, sustainable agriculture and food systems that empower vulnerable farmers, their families, and communities.
records.intermediaries: GAFSP is a Financial Intermediary Fund hosted within the World Bank Group, with the IBRD acting as trustee. Supervising entities such as the World Food Programme, ADB and FAO channeled the funds received from the IBRD to grantees.
records.implementers: Implementing partners include AfDB, ADB, IFAD, World Bank/IFC, FAO, WFP. Local partners include Asian Farmers Association for Sustainable Rural Development (AFA), ActionAid, CSOs, local organizations.
records.capital: Public, philathropic. Donors include Government of Australia, Canada, Germany, Ireland, Japan, Netherlands, Norway, Spain, UK, USA, Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation.
records.thematic: Thematic focus areas include climate resilience, women's empowerment, nutrition, and fragility, conflict, and violence (FCV), though they don't constitute separate funding programmes.
records.size:
Public Sector Grants (Country-Led): typically the largest, many projects ranging from USD 10 million - 30 million per grant.
Producer Organization-Led Grants: smaller-scale, designed for farmers' organizations - typical range between USD 2 million and USD 3 million per project. In 2025, the limit for national producer organizarions was USD 2.5 million, with higher amounts possible wherre applicants had an extensive track record in managin larger funds).

The GAFSP programme is active until 2030. Funding is typically provided for periods of up to 5 years, though the recommended  project duration is 3–4 years,
records.frequency:
GAFSP has issued 8 calls for proposals for producer organizations since 2010, the last being in 2025. GAFSP also has competitive calls for proposals for both the public and private sector. Calls are made a maximum of once per year.
- Public Sector Window: Provides grants for government-led projects.
- Private Sector Window (including BIFT): offers blended finance solutions for agribusinesses, typically in collaboration with partners like the IFC.
records.targetGroups:
Governments
Smallholders
Producer organizations
Small food system businesses · governments, smallholders, POs, SMEs, women
records.activities:
GAFSP provides financial and technical resources - investment grants, technical assistance and advisory services, as well as concessional finance - to results-driven food security and nutrition projects. Program resources help scale up financing for climate resilient practices, infrastructures, and technologies. Recent projects in Cambodia include a project to enhance the resilience and livelihoods of smallholder farmers through organic agriculture and access to markets, supported by WFP and the Cambodian Agriculture Cooperative Corporation (CACC).

In general, activities supported include:

Agricultural productivity/technology:
- Providing improved, climate-resilient seeds and fertilizers
- Implementing nutrition-sensitive agricultural activities, such as promoting biofortified crops
- Investing in irrigation systems and water management
- Supporting the adoption of climate-smart agricultural techniques

Value chain support:
- Enhancing rural infrastructure, such as access roads
- Developing post-harvest storage facilities and processing plants
- Linking smallholder farmers and producer organizations directly to local and regional markets and buyers.

Capacity building/technical assistance:
- Providing technical assistance and training to farmers on best practices, such as soil management and pest control
- Financial services, including microfinance, rural credit, and risk-sharing facilities (e.g., insurance) to farmers

In Cambodia, the Climate Resilience Rice Commercialization Sector Development Program (ADB) has helped increase smallholder farmers’ access to finance, equipment, and infrastructure that improves rice seed quality, yields, post-harvest technology, and export potential.
records.requirements:
Producer organizations (POs) must partner with a GAFSP supervising entity of their choice (e.g. Asian Development Bank, FAO, IFAD, World Bank, World Food Programme) and develop an Expression of Interest and a full proposal.

Eligibility criteria for the PO track grants include:
National/Subnational POs:
- Registered legal entity in a GAFSP-eligible country
- Operates nationally or subrationally in a GAFSP-eligible country
- Members include smallholder farmers, fishers, pastoralists, indigenous people etc.
- Provides services in agriculture, food, and nutrition security
- Member-owned and governed
Though NGOs are not included in this definition, in some countries, entities that are de facto POs must register as private companies or NGOs, and therefore eligibility is verified case-by-case based on whether the entity meets PO criteria.

Regional (Multi-country) POs
- Registered in a GAFSP-eligible or IDA blend country (this does not include Cambodia, therefore regional POs registered in Cambodia cannot apply)
- Operates in ≥2 GAFSP-eligible countries (activities limited to GAFSP-eligible countries)
- Members are mainly national POs meeting national PO criteria
- Supports members via capacity building, institutional development, etc.

Not eligible:
- National POs already implementing GAFSP-funded projects
- Ad hoc consortiums formed solely for application

Single Country Proposals
1. Must be implemented only in GAFSP-eligible countries
2. Must align with GAFSP goals and activities must support:
- Core areas: productivity, market linkages, risk reduction, rural livelihoods, institutions
- Cross-cutting outcomes: Climate resilience (mandatory), Women and girls' empowerment (mandatory), Nutrition (optional)
3. Build PO capacity (e.g., governance, financial, technical)
4. Must scale up at least one proven activity and include an innovative features
5. If civil works/assets: Must justify with clear rationale, context-fit, and exit strategy
6. If advocacy: Must be aligned with project objectives and within GAFSP’s mandate

Selection criteria for national POs include good governance, fiduciary and M&E capacity, operations and finance capacity (PO capacity), and technical quality, design feasbility, GAFSP alignment (proposal).
records.whoCanApply: Registered smallholder groups can access finance directly through the Producer Organization-led track.
records.enablingEnv:
Applicants: Applications must be made through supervising entities like FAO under the GAFSP framework.

Standards applicable to institutions involved: The environmental and social standards of the supervising entity administering a particular grant may be relevant to understand the enabling environment and potential environmental and social safeguards requirements. Additionally, since the GAFSP operates under the aegis of the World Bank Group, WBG policies may also be relevant.
records.notes:
Contact addresses: GAFSP General Inbox info@gafspfund.org
Shijie Yang – GAFSP Portfolio manager syang@worldbank.org
Cecilia Magarotto – PO Portfolio Lead cmagarotto@worldbank.org
Relevant sub-programmes of the GAFSP include the Business Investment Financing Track Pilot (BIFT), designed to catalyze access to affordable private and climate finance for smallholder farmers, producer organizations, innovative startups, and micro-, small-, and medium-enterprises (MSMEs) in the agrifood sector.

records.name: Global Centre on Biodiversity for Climate
records.summary: The Global Centre on Biodiversity for Climate (GCBC) is a UK Official Development Assistance programme that supports developing countries in shaping decisions and policies that better value, protect, restore, and sustainably manage biodiversity while strengthening climate resilience and supporting poverty alleviation. It operates in ODA-eligible countries in Latin America and the Caribbean, Sub-Saharan Africa, South-East Asia and the Pacific, or Small Island Developing States.
records.intermediaries: GCBC is funded by the UK’s Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) with International Climate Finance and managed in partnership with DAI (international development consultancy).
records.implementers: Grants are implemented directly by recipients.
records.capital: Public, UK-funded ODA programme.
records.thematic: climate change mitigation and adaptation, biodiversity
records.size: £ 100,000 and £1 million was offered in the last cycle, for projects of 12-36 months duration
records.frequency: once or twice a year since 2024, third round recently concluded
records.targetGroups: researchers working with indigenous and local communities · researchers
records.activities: One of the themes in the last call for applications was on using biodiversity to improve the climate resilience of agricultural, food and bioeconomy value chains.
records.requirements:
Requirements for the most recent call for applications included:
- GESI: All proposals must incorporate clear plans to factor in gender, equality and social inclusion from the outset, as well as equitable access and benefit sharing
- R&D: Proposed work must meet the definition of research and development: creative and systematic work undertaken to increase the stock of knowledge and to devise new applications of available knowledge
- Research should aim to generate learning, solutions, tools or methodologies that can be upscaled and replicated in other regions or countries.
- Innovation encouraged
- the value of any individual grant may not exceed 25% of the applicant’s or Lead Consortia’s Partner’s average income/turnover for the past 3 years.
- non-government organisations, civil society organisations, multilateral organisations, social development organisations, academic institutions, private sector partners  were eligible to apply (as well as parastatal organizations, if the proposed activities are not receiving funding from other governments)
- Any proposed offer from a consortium should be headed by a single Lead Delivery Partner. Prospective Lead Delivery Partners will lead and submit applications on behalf of all members of their consortium.
- Applications for project concept(s) must be:
 - led by an Organisation with offices in an ODA eligible country, or
 - led by an Organisation which forms part of a consortium with Organisations that have an office in an ODA eligible country or countries.
- The GCBC encourages applications from the Lead Delivery Partners/Organisations based in our target ODA-eligible country (including Cambodia). New and equitable partnerships involving local project Partners  encouraged.
- Private sector Partners may be consortia members, but are ineligible to receive grant funds for profit, or act as consortia Lead Delivery Partners.
- PhD Students not eligible for funding
records.whoCanApply: Farmer cooperatives and producer organizations may be eligible to apply if applications remain open to non-government organisations, civil society organisations, and social development organisations
records.enablingEnv:
Underlying programmes, policies and conventions: The programme is part of the UK Official Development Assistance programme. GCBC builds on the UK’s Dasgupta Review and helps countries achieve a nature-positive future by supporting commitments made by the UK government at UNFCCC COP26 and the 15th UN Biodiversity Conference, as well as supporting delivery of the Sustainable Development Goals.

Applicants: Explicit requirements regarding legal structure were not identified, but for consortia applications, lead organizations are required to have offices in ODA-eligible countries.

Standards applicable to institutions involved: All proposals must incorporate clear plans to factor in gender, equality and social inclusion from the outset, as well as equitable access and benefit sharing

records.name: Canadian Climate and Nature Fund for the Private Sector in Asia
records.summary: This fund established by the Canadian government aims to stimulate private sector investment in climate and nature-based solutions (NbS) projects that advance gender equality across Asia and the Pacific, especially in developing countries and small island developing states.
records.intermediaries: The fund is financed by the Government of Canada through Global Affairs Canada.
records.implementers: ADB is the trustee and manager of the fund.
records.capital: Public.
records.instruments: concessional debt instruments, including senior and subordinated loans, mezzanine financing (debt) instruments, and guarantees · Loans/debt, guarantees
records.thematic: clean energy,NbS and biodiversity, climate-smart agriculture, climate governance
records.size: The total fund size is CAD 360 million. ADB will deploy capital over a 7-year investment period followed by an implementation period of up to 20 years. ADB will blend the fund’s resources with its ordinary capital resources.
records.frequency: Not open for direct applications by farmer groups.
records.targetGroups: private enterprises working with NbS · private enterprises
records.activities:
Target activities include:
(i) reducing emissions and transitioning away from high carbon pathways to improve resilience to climate change;
(ii) financing NbS to protect, sustainably manage, and restore natural or modified ecosystems.
This includes:
Habitat restoration and protection
Sustainable aquaculture
Sustainable (climate-smart) agriculture
Pollution prevention and water management
Nature protection and ecotourism
records.requirements:
Eligible countries: projects across ADB developing member countries if eligible for official development assistance at the time of ADB approval. Eligible countries include low-income and lower and upper middle-income
countries, including small island developing states.
Eligible recipients: The fund will finance entities that satisfy ADB’s criteria for nonsovereign financing.
records.whoCanApply: Not open for direct applications.
records.enablingEnv: Standards applicable to institutions involved and underlying policies and programes: ADB policies, for example on gender equality. In particular, all financed projects will be screened using a framework of methodologies developed jointly with other multilateral development banks to help ensure projects meet low-carbon and climate-resilient standards consistent with the UNFCCC Paris Agreement. For financed NBS projects, ADB will follow the common principles for tracking nature-positive finance announced at UNFCCC COP 28.

records.name: GIZ
records.summary: German development agency that provides services for international cooperation and sustainable development across more than 130 countries.
records.intermediaries: These include the German Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ), German Federal Ministry for the Environment, Nature Conservation and Nuclear Safety (BMU), the German Federal Foreign Office, and the European Union. GIZ provides funding through local organizations, public institutions, and NGOs. Financial partners and intermediaries are also used, including commerical banks and micro-finance institutions.
records.implementers: For Cambodia, implementing partners include the ASEAN Secretariat, the Cambodian Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries and Provincial Departments of Environment.
records.capital: Public. GIZ is primarily funded by the German government.
records.instruments: Grants, concessional loans, climate risk insurance · Grants, loans/debt, insurance/de-risking products
records.thematic:
GIZ focus areas are broad, and include:
- Agricultural innovation & technology
- Sustainable supply chains
- Training and advisory services
- Climate resilience
- Emergency aid and food security
records.size: Highly variable depending on size and location - grants range from USD 100,000 to 10,000,000 or more.
records.frequency: GIZ publishes periodic calls for proposals, but largely works directly with local partners to identify and implement projects aligned with its objectives.
records.targetGroups:
Smallholder farmers
Agriculturar cooperatives
Processers
Traders
Agri-SMEs
Input providers
Microfinance institutions · smallholders, cooperatives, processors, traders, SMEs, input providers, MFIs
records.activities:
GIZ activity areas are broad, and include:
- Agricultural digitalization
- Agricultural mechanisation
- Pest management
- Value chain development
- Deforestation free agriculture
- Farmer field schools
- Financial literacy
- Extension services
- Climate adaptation practices
- Soil and water management
- Biodiversity conservation
records.requirements: Recipients must be commercially and legally eligible to use the financing properly. GIZ may also check the environmental and social compatibility of the measures to be financed.
records.whoCanApply: Farmers cannot access finance directly from GIZ; funding is provided to local partner organisations, NGOs, SMEs, financial institutions or local governments.
records.enablingEnv: Underlying programmes and policies: GIZ finance complies with the public-benefit rules set out in the German Fiscal Code and the EU rules on state aid. GIZ decisions are guided by standards such as the United Nations Global Compact and the German Sustainability Code.
records.notes: Relevant active projects include the EU-German Cambodia Partnership for Sustainable Agriculture and Food Systems (EU-German CAPSAFE) and Promotion of Sustainable Agricultural Value-Chains in ASEAN II (ASEAN AgriTrade II).

records.name: IKI Small Grants
records.summary: The IKI Small Grants programme is a German government-funded initiative that supports local, regional, and national organizations in ODA-eligible countries to implement small-scale projects tackling climate change and biodiversity loss.
records.intermediaries: The programme relies on national and regional institutions to act as intermediaries, which are responsible for managing their own calls for proposals, selecting projects, and implementing, monitoring, and providing technical support to local organizations.
records.implementers: GIZ
records.capital: Public. Funded by the German government.
records.thematic: support small-scale, local, or regional climate and biodiversity action
records.size: Grants range between EUR 60,000 to 200,000 per project, and are typically provided for a duration of 1-3 years.
records.frequency: Funding calls are made annually.
records.targetGroups: Small NGOs, Local/national institutions · NGOs, governments
records.activities:
Activities funded include:
- Climate-smart agriculture
- Sustainable land management
- Renewable energy in agriculture
- Water harvesting and management
- Value chain development
- Agricultural digitalisation
records.requirements: Applicants must have been operative for at least 3 years and have an average annual revenue of EUR 60,000 to EUR 500,000.
records.whoCanApply: Regional, national and local organisations based in ODA countries can apply.
records.enablingEnv:
Underlying programmes and policies: GIZ finance complies with the public-benefit rules set out in the German Fiscal Code and the EU rules on state aid. GIZ decisions are guided by standards such as the United Nations Global Compact and the German Sustainability Code.

Standards applicable: IKI has an Independent Complaint Mechanism that focusses on:
- monitoring and improving the environmental and social outcomes of projects
- avoiding unintended negative impacts of projects
- supporting the appropriate use of public funds, and
- complying with international good practice.
records.notes: Call closed for 2026 for small, large and medium grants.

records.name: International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD)
records.summary: IFAD is a specialised UN agency and an international financial institution dedicated to mobilising resources for agriculture and rural development in developing countries.
records.intermediaries: IFAD often partners with local NGOs, financial intermediaries or other local entities to implement projects.
records.implementers: Typically the national government in partnership with local partners. Examples include the Cambodian Ministry of Water Resources and Meteorology, National Committee for Sub-National Democratic Development, Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries and Ministry of Rural Development.
records.capital: Blended, including public and philanthropy. IFAD is funded by over 170 member states.
records.thematic: rural and agricultural development, climate change mitigation and adaptation
records.size:
Small grants < USD 500,000
Large grants > USD 500,000

The cost of ongoing IFAD co-financed projects in Cambodia is between USD 90-250 million.
records.frequency: Regular proposal calls throughout the year, usually structured around a thematic grant programme.
records.targetGroups:
Rural communities
Small-scale farmers
Local communities
Indigenous Peoples · smallholders, local communities, IPLC, youth, women
records.activities:
Climate smart agriculture
Improved water management
Connecting small-scale farmers to markets
Rural banking
Biodiversity protection

Key activities in Cambodia include:
Enabling poor smallholders to take advantage of market opportunities;
Increasing resilience to climate change and other shocks in poor rural households and communities;
Improving poor households' access to rural services.
records.requirements: The grant application procedure appears to be based on the advertised calls. Eligible recipients must have been legally constituted in an IFAD Member State. For loans, IFAD assesses lending terms for borrowing countries based on their GNI per capita and creditworthiness assessment by IFAD.
records.whoCanApply: Recipients of IFAD grants can include developing Member States, intergovernmental organizations (including United Nations agencies), civil society organizations, research and academic institutions, producer organizations, foundations and private companies. For lending, IFAD uses a performance-based allocation system (PBAS) to distribute funding to projects, which determines how much financing to allocate to a country based on its needs, performance and vulnerability.
records.enablingEnv:
Underlying policies and programmes, and applicable standards:
All IFAD projects are aligned with and operate in the context of the Cambodian Government's national development strategies, in particular the Agriculture Sector Master Plan 2030 (ASMP), Cambodia's NDC under the Paris Agreement, Climate Change Strategic Plan 2014–2023 and the Roadmap for Food Systems for Sustainable Development 2030, Five-year Strategic Plan for strengthening gender mainstreaming and women’s empowerment, National Policy on the Development of Indigenous Peoples, and National Water Resources Management and Sustainable Irrigation Road Map and Investment Program 2019–2033, as mentioned in the IFAD Cambodia Country Strategic Opportunities Programme 2022–2027 (CSOP). Further information can be found in the section "Social, Environmental and Climate Assessment Procedure (SECAP) background study".

The CSOP further details the various national laws, regulations, and commitments at the national and international level that are relevant to meeting IFAD objectives, such as on environmental, biodiversity and climate protection, land degradation prevention, land tenure, Indigenous Peoples, water resources management and sustainable irrigation, gender, youth, and persons with disabilities.
records.notes: Last year, a grant call was issued related to community-level capacity and regional cooperation on One Health for livestock and communities in the Mekong region. 4 IFAD co-financed projects are currently ongoing in Cambodia (Climate Adaptive Irrigation and Sustainable Agriculture for Resilience- CAISAR; Accelerating Inclusive Markets for Smallholders-AIMS, Agriculture Services Programme for an Inclusive Rural Economy and Agricultural Trade-ASPIRE-AT, and Sustainable Assets for Agriculture Markets, Business and Trade Project-SAAMBAT). It may be worth contacting responsible officers to inquire about integration of smallholder organizations into ongoing or upcoming programmes (Rachel Arcese, Country Director. r.arcese@ifad.org and Frew Behabtu, Country Director, f.behabtu@ifad.org)

records.name: Swiss Investment Fund for Emerging Markets (SIFEM)
records.summary: SIFEM is the Swiss DFI and manages and grows a portfolio that invests in profit-oriented small and medium-sized enterprises, as well as fast-growing companies through financial intermediaries to facilitate  sustainable and inclusive economic growth. It operates in countries across the globe including 40+ priority countries.
records.intermediaries: SIFEM invests in fund managers like LeapFrog Investments (Leapfrog Climate Fund), and provides loans to financial intermediaries such as local banks, leasing companies, micro-financing companies and other financial institutions.
records.capital: Public: funded by the Swiss government
records.instruments: Equity in SME-oriented funds (usually funds providing equity to SMEs, occassionally funds that lend to SMEs); loans and advisory services to financial intermediaries; quasi-equity instruments; guarantees · Equity, loans/debt, guarantees
records.thematic: SIFEM's general investment criteria include employment generation,  inclusive goods and services, and climate change mitigation or adaptation.
records.size: Recent worldwide investments in the agriculture, fisheries and forestry sectors have been to the tune of USD 10-15 million, with some having a clear time frame of 2-3 years. The maximum exposure in a single company should not exceed 3% of SIFEM’s total capital commitments at the time of investment.
records.frequency: SIFEM encourages fund managers and financial institutions to connect but does not consider requests for direct project funding or direct company funding.
records.targetGroups: Profit-oriented SMEs and fast-growing companies · SMEs
records.activities: Activities in the agri-food sector include curbing deforestation and land degradation and  promoting sustainable rural value chains and livelihoods, including those of indigenous and smallholder communities
records.requirements:
Recipients are usually SME-oriented funds (usually funds providing equity to SMEs, and occassionally funds that lend to SMEs).  The maximum exposure in a single company shall not exceed 3% of SIFEM’s total capital commitments at the time of investment.
For equity investments, SIFEM requires that the funding structure of the investee is well-balanced and normally takes significant minority stakes in the portfolio company. The strategic partners in the project must be willing to enter a long-term commitment with a relevant risk exposure.For its equity and quasi-equity investments, SIFEM seeks a market return.
General requirements outlined in the Investment Guidelines 2020 include the following:
- Active local participation is desirable. The local partner shall have a sound knowledge of local conditions, experience of the business involved, and a material financial interest in the enterprise.
- SIFEM’s investments must primarily be used to finance specific projects or investment programs aiming at modernizing and expanding the portfolio companies, or for their permanent working capital requirements.
- For the selection of investment projects, key business factors considered include:
the expertise and reputation of the management team and the sponsor,
the prospect for the industry in which the portfolio company is active,
the competitive advantages (including barriers to entry) and profitability of the product range,
the company’s growth potential,
strong governance and financial controls,
clear alignment with the sponsor/owners regarding SIFEM’s exit.
records.whoCanApply: Funds are usually targeted at SMEs and routed through specialized investment funds and local financial institutions.
records.enablingEnv:
Standards applicable to institutions involved: SIFEM encourages high standards of corporate governance, social responsibility, occupational health and safety as well as respect for human rights and the external environment. This should be in dialogue with partners such as communities in which the portfolio companies are located, management, staff, investors, co-financiers and business partners.
SIFEM’s Approach to Responsible Investment stipulates SIFEM’s ESG-related investment requirements. It has been based on international accepted, best practice standards which include
- the UN Guiding Principles for Business and Human Rights
- ILO Core Labour Standards
- International Finance Corporation’s Standards on Social and Environmental Sustainability (2012) and the associated Environmental, Health and Safety (EHS) Guidelines
- the Corporate Governance Development Framework
- the Client Protection Principles
- the OECD Convention on Combating Bribery of Foreign Public Officials in International Business Transactions

records.name: Dutch Fund for Climate and Development (DFCD) Origination Facility
records.summary: The Dutch Fund for Climate and Development (DFCD) is a climate resilience fund, dedicated to supporting climate adaptation and mitigation projects which benefit vulnerable communities and landscapes. The DFCD Origination Facility identifies promising climate-focused projects in vulnerable countries throughout Africa, Asia, and Latin America and helps them develop into scalable, bankable solutions.
records.intermediaries: FMO (Dutch Entrepreneurial Development Bank), CFM (Climate Fund Managers), SNV (Netherlands Development Agency), WWF Netherlands.
records.capital: Public: funded by the Dutch government
records.instruments: Blended finance, grants, debt, and equity · Blended finance, grants, loans/debt, equity
records.size: Recent grant funding in Cambodia was between EUR 100,000 to 300,000. The fund aims to raise USD 2 billion in funding and by the end of 2027, to have 55 projects contracted and 34 graduated to the Land Use or Water investment facilities.
records.frequency: Investment opportunities are identified by WWF and SNV through the Origination Facility. It is also possible to apply directly at any time.
records.targetGroups: Companies in the following high-impact sectors: Forestry, Agriculture, Water and Sanitation Hygiene, and Environmental Protection. Investments in the agriculture sector in Cambodia have had a focus on benefitting smallholder farmers. · private enterprises
records.activities: Origination Facility (OF) funding can be put towards activities such as feasibility studies, due diligence work, environmental and social safeguard checks, pilots to prove concept, or assistance to develop business models, and forms a pipeline generator for the Water and Land Use Facilities. OF projects in Cambodia have included investing in agri-tech companies engaged in the production of biochar‑based, crop‑specific fertilisers, introduction of agroforestry in coffee production, and climate-resilient, circular mango processing.
records.requirements:
Eligibility criteria for applicants include the following (more details on the Origination Facility page):
- the lead organisation receiving funding should be a private sector entity and have total value of assets or annual turnover of at least €5 million
- the initiative has the potential to scale up with a long-term finance need of at least €5 million
- the initiative should be able to co-invest, cash/in kind via own or external resources.
- projects must be from an eligible country and allign with national development goals
- projects must positively impact climate adaptation and some or all of the following: Biodiversity, Food and Nutrition Security, Gender Equality and Social Inclusion

- The Origination Facility is responsible for project identification and (pre-) feasibility development activities.
- The Land Use Facility targets investments which have graduated from the Origination Facility in sectors relating to agroforestry, sustainable land use and climate resilient food production.
- The Water Use Facility targets investments which have graduated from the Origination Facility in sectors related to water and sanitation infrastructure, as well as environmental protection.
records.whoCanApply: Applicants must be private sector entities so individual farmers and producers cannot directly apply.
records.enablingEnv:
Relevant policies and programmes: The project must be aligned with national development plans and priorities of the host country.
Applicant requirements: Applicants must be private sector entities.
Standards applicable: The principal objective of the project must be to improve climate adaptation or mitigation according to the OECD Rio Marker 2 methodology.

records.name: Reversing Environmental Degradation in Africa and Asia (REDAA)
records.summary: REDAA is a programme that supports research and action in sub-Saharan Africa and South and Southeast Asia by offering grants and facilitating mutual learning between partners.  Funded initiatives are locally led, interdisciplinary, and focused on solutions for ecosystem restoration and climate resilience, enabling people and nature to thrive. Projects can aim to improve evidence, apply new tools or strengthen governance systems to support nature-positive actions, enhance local livelihoods and tackle the impacts of climate change.
records.intermediaries: REDAA is funded by UK International Development from the UK’s Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office.
records.implementers: REDAA is managed by the International Institute for Environment and Development (IIED).
records.capital: Public.
records.thematic: nature restoration and climate resilience
records.size:
Catalytic grants between £50,000 and £100,000 ( 6 - 12 months).
Medium-scale project grants between £200,000 and £500,000 (2 - 4 years).
Large-scale programme grants between £1,000,000 and £1,500,000 (over 4 years).
records.frequency:
Catalytic grants: One or two rounds likely between 2026-2028. Each grant round is likely to fund between 6 and 12 proposals.
Medium-scale grants: First round issued in 2023, next round unclear.
Large-scale grants: further grants unlikely to be issued.
records.targetGroups:
Local communities and vulnerable groups, including Indigenous Peoples, women, youth, migrant workers and landless labourers. Geographical areas prioritized in Cambodia include:
- Tonle Sap, UNESCO World Heritage Site
- Prey Lang and the Eastern Plains Landscape · local communities, IPLC, women, youth
records.activities:
REDAA offers grants and, in some cases, technical support, to organisations that already have proven and effective systems for supporting the actions of Indigenous Peoples and local communities. REDAA-funded initiatives address gender equality and social inclusion, climate resilience and action for nature, and each is focused on one or more of the following main thematic priorities:
Local research and capability for research
Resource and land use assessments
Business models
Financing mechanisms
Inclusive governance systems

Target environments include peatlands and other terrestrial wetlands, mangroves, coastal lands, rivers, forests, farm-forest landscapes, drylands, uplands and mountains, and urban and peri-urban areas. For instance, projects in Cambodia have focussed on strengthening Indigenous land management for improved agroecology and wetland governance.
records.requirements:
Lead organisations must be able to demonstrate that they are:
- A non-profit organisation, which may be a non-governmental organisation, research institution or community-based organisation that is a legally registered entity
- Experienced in the kind of work they propose to undertake
- Financially sound
- Staffed with the appropriate technical and financial capacity and expertise to manage and implement projects successfully and deliver technical and financial reporting.

Lead organisations based within one of the three focal regions (sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia or Southeast Asia) will be prioritised for funding.

Lead organisations may form partnerships with one or more additional organisations. In projects where partner organisations are involved, the project should be co-designed with those partners.

Organisations eligible for REDAA funding in wider partnerships include:
- Non-profit organisations, which may be non-governmental organisations, research institutions or community-based organisations
- Private sector organisations, businesses or business associations, which may be sub-granted (or contracted via a consultancy agreement) to undertake specific planned actions for the programme, provided this partnership can demonstrate value for money in its costs and benefits to the programme.

Government, intergovernmental and UN agencies are not eligible to receive funding from REDAA. However, these agencies may be key programme partners.

Applications will be made through IIED’s Flexigrant system.
records.whoCanApply: Grants may be accessed by farmer or producer groups, especially if they apply through  legally registered community-based organisations, either as lead or partner organizatins depending on ability to demonstrate tehcnical and financial capacity.
records.enablingEnv:
Observations on relevant policies and programmes: The focus areas of funding interventions include improving tenure security and resource rights of Indigenous Peoples and local communities, and improving citizen participation in law- and policy-making, and thus also potentially engaging with underlying laws, regulations and policies to strengthen them.

Applicant requirements: The lead organizations must be a non-profit organisation, which may be a non-governmental organisation, research institution or community-based organisation that is a legally registered entity.

Standards applicable: REDAA uses the REDAA Gender Equality and Social Inclusion (GESI) continuum to help project implementers assess intersectional ineqalities and enhance social equity.

records.name: Mobilising Finance For Forests (MFF) Program
records.summary: The MFF program is a blended finance investment program to combat deforestation and other environmentally unsustainable land use practices in tropical regions in Southeast Asia, Latin America and Africa.
records.geo: tropical regions in Southeast Asia, Latin America and Africa
records.intermediaries: The MFF program is funded by the UK and Netherlands governments.
records.implementers: The Dutch development bank FMO is the implementing agency of this program.
records.capital: While the MFF comprises public funds (EUR 178 million (GBP 150 million) from the UK government), the objective is to mobilize private finace (EUR 1 billion) for forestry and sustainable land use projects through catalytic investments.
records.instruments: Equity, debt, technical assistance · Equity, loans/debt
records.thematic: nature-based solutions to tackle the drivers of climate change and biodiversity loss, protect and restore critical ecosystems; build resilience, just rural transition towards sustainable land use
records.size:
MFF offers long term financing up to 15 years to a mix of fund and direct investments.  Up to 20% of the funding can be used for early stage project development.

Fund investments in 3 to 5 Funds (70-80% of the program):
Investment funds targeting sustainable investments in the forestry and other land-use sectors
Equity or debt investments
Direct investments (20-30% of program)
Minority shares in equity investments
Loans of up to (the equivalent of) EUR 10 million
records.frequency: The selection process does not appear to be call-based.
records.targetGroups: Fund managers, forest-related projects · fund managers
records.activities:
The MFF targets:
- Projects that increase the value of standing forests to lower the incentive to cut down forests (e.g. harvesting non-timber forest products such as nuts, seeds or native forest coffee, carbon offsetting schemes, eco tourism, conservation projects).
- Projects that integrate forest protection and restoration into agricultural production to reduce deforestation pressure (e.g soy, cattle, palm oil, cocoa, timber).
records.whoCanApply: It does not appear that farmers and small-scale producers can access funding directly.
records.enablingEnv:
Relevant policies and standards applicable: All MFF transactions are reviewed by FMO’s investment and credit functions. FMO as per its Sustainability Policy requires all customers to comply with applicable environmental, social and human rights laws in their home and host countries. FMO also upholds the following (inter)national standards, including in its own operations, as applicable:
- IFC Performance Standards / World Bank Group Environmental Health and Safety Guidelines
- OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises
- UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights
- ILO Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work
- UN Principles for Responsible Investment
- UN Principles for Responsible Banking
- EDFI Principles for Responsible Financing of Sustainable Development
- G20/OECD Principles of Corporate Governance
- Dutch Corporate Governance Code
- CFI Client Protection Principles
- Operating Principles for Impact Management
- Corporate Governance Development Framework
records.notes: MFF focuses on tropical forest countries, with Tier 1 countries (receiving at least 50% of funding) including Brazil, Colombia, Peru, Ghana, Ivory Coast, Republic of Congo, DRC, Gabon, Indonesia, and Malaysia. Tier 2 countries include Mexico, Paraguay, Ecuador, Nigeria, Ethiopia, Kenya, Tanzania, Mozambique, Zambia, South Africa, India, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, and the Philippines.

records.name: Critical Ecosystem Partnership Fund Indo-Burma Hotspot
records.summary: This funding opportunity supports civil society-led initiatives in the Indo-Burma region that strengthen protected area governance, integrate biodiversity into development planning, and build the capacity of local organizations, with grants ranging from USD 50,000 to USD 250,000.
records.intermediaries: CEPF is a joint initiative of l’Agence Française de Développement, Conservation International, the European Union, Fondation Hans Wilsdorf, the Global Environment Facility, the Government of Canada, the Government of Japan and the World Bank. In the Indo-Burma Hotspot, it is also supported by Margaret A. Cargill Philanthropies.
records.implementers: IUCN is leading the Regional Implementation Team for the latest application cycle for the Indo-Burma Biodiversity Hotspot.
records.capital: Blended, including public and philanthropic donors mentioned as intermediary institutions.
records.thematic: biodiversity, livelihoods, nature-based solutions
records.size: small grants (up to USD 50,000) and large grants (USD 50,000 to 250,000). Funded projects are usually 1-2 years in length, and large grants may be for longer periods where needed.
records.frequency: The fund is currently in its fourth cycle since 2000.
records.targetGroups: Indigenous People and Local Communities · IPLC, youth, women
records.activities:
Strategic directions and related investment priorities based on the latest round of funding include:
3. Strengthen the management effectiveness of Protected and Conserved Areas (PCAs) and the engagement of CSOs and Indigenous People and Local Communities (IPs and LCs) in their management and governance to improve conservation at priority sites.
Investment priorities:
- Empower IPs and LCs and CSOs to participate in the governance of PCAs and to strengthen their rights and opportunities in broader resource management.
- Enhance PCA effectiveness through the adoption of global standards and the development of accredited training programmes.
- Empower IPs and LCs to lead and sustain Other Effective Area-based Conservation Measures (OECMs) through authentic local processes.

6. Implement scalable approaches for integrating biodiversity, ecosystem services and Nature-based Solutions (NbS) into development planning in priority corridors.
Investment priorities:
- Assess development policies and their impacts on biodiversity and ecosystem services and promote alternative scenarios, NbS and mitigation measures.
- Implement and scale ecosystem restoration efforts, including demonstration projects, to generate replicable models and inform broader application.
- Engage the media to increase awareness, inform public debate and influence decision-making on mainstreaming biodiversity into development planning.

9. Support the establishment, capacity and organisational development of civil society organisations to work on biodiversity, communities and livelihoods at regional, national, local and grassroots levels.
Investment priorities:
- Support networking and knowledge exchange mechanisms, including mentoring partnerships between established CSOs and new or informal groups, that enable collective civil society responses to priority and emerging threats.
records.requirements:
Preference is  given to projects that:
(i) are the closest fit to investment priorities (see Target activities)
(ii) have a high likelihood of achieving their stated objectives and contribute strongly to sustainable conservation outcomes;
(iii) build upon past initiatives and complement ongoing initiatives;
(iv) represent good value for money; and
(v) demonstrate the institutional capacity and experience necessary to carry out the work.
Eligible applicants must:
- Be a legally recognized civil society organization with its own bank account and which is eligible to receive charitable contributions under relevant national laws
- Operate in one or more eligible Indo-Burma countries
- Propose projects aligned with CEPF investment priorities
- Demonstrate institutional and technical capacity to deliver results
- Collaborate with communities, IPs, LCs, or relevant stakeholders
- Public universities and organizations must demonstrate that they have a legal personality independent of any government agency or sector, the authority to apply for and receive private funds, and must not be in a position to assert a claim of sovereign immunity.

Eligibility criteria differ based on the theme of the proposal and the strategic direction of the fund it aligns with. Based on the latest call, these include:
Strategic Direction 3: management effectiveness of Protected and Conserved Areas (PCAs):
(i) focus on one or more of the  priority sites in listed in the Ecosystem Profile;
(ii) demonstrate wellbeing benefits for local communities.
Projects must also apply gender-responsive management practices that support women to increase their access to natural resources, as well as their participation in environmental decision making.

Strategic Direction 6: integrating biodviersity, ecosystem services and NbS into development planning in priority corridors:
(i) demonstrate scalable approaches that are suitable for replication by civil society or private sector actors, or for incorporation into government programmes;
(ii) focus on one or more of the five priority corridors  listed in the Ecosystem Profile.

Strategic Direction 9: organisational development of civil society organisations:
(i) integrate gender considerations into their design and implementation and demonstrate strategies to promote equity in access to capacity building and organisational development;
(ii) ensure that the perspectives of women, Indigenous Peoples, youth and marginalized groups are embedded in coalitions and advocacy.
records.whoCanApply: Non-governmental organisations, community groups, Indigenous People’s organisations, women’s groups, private companies, small businesses, and other local civil society organisations (CSOs) can apply if legally registered.
records.enablingEnv:
Applicants: must be legally registered organizations based on applicable national laws.

Standards applicable to institutions involved: The CEPF has environmental and social safeguard policies concerning labour and working conditions, resettlement, biodviersity conservation, Indigenous Peoples, pollution prevention, community health and safety, cultural heritage, gender mainstreaming and stakeholder engagement, set out in the Environmental and Social Management Framework. Projects are reviewed before and during implementation to prevent adverse impacts in these areas.

The latest application phase was live until March 16 2026. Contact address: Mary Ann Bayang, Climate Change, Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities Specialist, UNDP: mary.ann.bayang@undp.org
Nina Kantcheva, Senior Policy Adviser, Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities Engagement: nina.kantcheva@undp.org

records.name: Keidanren Nature Conservation Fund (KNCF) Grant Program
records.summary: The KNCF is a Japanese fund that supports nature conservation by NGOs and other nonprofit organizations in developing countries, particularly in the Asia-Pacific region.
records.intermediaries: The fund is supervised by the Japanese Ministry of Environment and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Sumitomo Trust and Banking Co is the trustee of the fund and the Keidanren Nature Conservation Council is responsible for fundraising.
records.capital: Blended. KNCF is funded by the member corporations of Nippon Keidanren (the Japanese Business Federation) and the general public.
records.thematic: biodiversity protection and its synergies with sustainable development
records.size:
Recent grants average about JPY 3 million. Grants are for one year, renewable on an annual basis for a maximum of three additional years. In particular, the Fund supports:
1) small-scale projects (projects applying for less than JPY 1 million/year) given for 1 year, renewable annually for 3 more years.
i) organizations applying to the KNCF for the first time and
ii) grassroots NGOs in UN-designated least developed countries (which includes Cambodia)
2) medium-scale projects (up to JPY 10 million/year) given for 3 years
3) large-scale projects (up to JPY 20 million/year) given for 3 years
records.frequency: KNCF announces an annual request for grant applications.
records.targetGroups: NGOs and CSOs · NGOs, CSOs
records.activities: A recently funded project in Cambodia pertained to protecting the habitat of the Sarus Crane and contributing to improving faramers livelihoods through crane-friendly rice production practices. Other projects include developing alternate income sources for farmers to prevent oil palm plantation expansion in Indonesia.
records.requirements:
Applications have to be made through the KNCF grant management system.

Medium-scale projects should either be in their initial stages or to offer new approaches to solving problems. Large-scale projects should be collaborative projects involving multiple NGOs, preferably involving cooperation with local society and businesses. General requirements include:
(1) Appropriate cooperation has been obtained from the government organizations, related international organizations, NGOs and residents in the locations of the target projects.
(2) The results do not benefit any organization or individual.
(3) The project is implemented by experts with scientific knowledge, or the advice and cooperation of experts with scientific knowledge has been obtained in implementing the project.
(4) The applicant must be an organization that satisfies the following conditions:
- It can appropriately report its activities, budgets and financial status of granted projects.
- It has incorporated status or is a voluntary organization with societal credibility equivalent to an incorporated organization.
- It has a record of conducting nature conservation projects for 3 years or more.
- Applicants must submit financial statements or certified audits for the past 3 years, and for incorporated organizations, documents that show proof of such incorporation (does not apply to small-scale grants). Note: It is unclear if the exemption extends only to proof of incorporation or also to financial statements.
records.whoCanApply: The Fund targets NGOs and CSOs that are active in nature conservation projects, which may include farmer cooperatives and producer organizations.
records.enablingEnv:

records.name: Samdhana Institute
records.summary: Samdhana is a grants facilitator working in the socio-environmental movement in Southeast Asia, and also offers technical expertise to support grassroots movers in accessing resources for community-defined and community-led efforts in development.
records.intermediaries: Samdhana facilitates grants from a range of donors like Global Greengrants and World Bank. It also continues to collaborate closely with other grant-giving organizations that originally were funded by Global Greengrants, such as Fondo Casa and Fondo Acción Solidaria.
records.implementers: Grants are implemented directly by recipients.
records.capital: Blended. Samdhana faciltiates grants from a range of donors.
records.thematic: natural resource management, climate change mitigation and adaptation, livelihoods, governance, disability rights,
records.size:
Micro Grant: USD 500-10,000
Small Grant: USD 10,000 - 30,000
These can be granted for projects implemented for over 6 months to 1 year.
Urgent action grants of up to USD 3,000 are made available for requests that are time-critical and considered as emergencies or life-threatening.
records.frequency: No open calls for proposals for projects in Cambodia. Applications can be submitted directly or organizations can be introduced through a "chain of trust" comprising Samdhana staff and partner organizations. Communities and partners may reach out as the need arises, and Samdhana personnel assist them with the proposal preparation and other requirements.
records.targetGroups: community-based groups, CSOs and other local organizations · CSOs
records.activities: Core operations are anchored on the process of trust-building, facilitation and assistance to IPs and LCs in preparing their proposals to address strategically the concerns and problems they face, and capacity development support to grantee-partners. Community needs and concerns are paramount in the determination of what Samdhana supports through its grants and capacity development programs.
records.requirements: Samdhana personnel assist communities with proposal preparation and other requirements.  Proposals and requests can be written in local languages, and other requirements usually called for by traditional funders (such as government accreditation or a bank account) can be dispensed with. Community partners are not required to be formally registered entities and can be indigenous organizations  established based on traditional political systems or modes of governance. Samdhana also supports informal community groups with clear plans around short term projects.
records.whoCanApply: Farmer cooperatives and producer organizations may be able to access grants, irrespective of formal registration, size and structure.
records.enablingEnv:
Applicants: formal legal registration is not required. Informal community groups and customary groups can also apply for grants.

Standards applicable to institutions involved: donor requirements might inform the capacity development programs of community partners. For example, some ask for Gender Equality and Social Inclusion (GESI) information or financial management provisions. In these cases, training can be made available for most, if not all, community partners.
