records.name: Conservation International Community Fishery Conservation Trust Fund scheme
records.summary: CI helps Community Fisheries organizations (CFis) and women's savings groups (WSGs) in Cambodia set up interconnected trust funds/sustainable finance schemes to strengthen their capacity, confidence, and autonomy.
records.intermediaries: The trust funds are managed by the recipient Cfis with the help of local banks.
records.capital: Blended. Initial grants are made from CI funds which constitute a mix of public, private and philanthropic donors.
records.instruments: Grant, which is deposited as an interest-generating deposit in the bank, and catalyzes other funding sources such as from partner women savings groups and local governments. · Grants
records.thematic: sustainable fisheries
records.size: The capital value of the conservation trust fund can vary, but CI estimated USD 5000 to be the average minimum viable amount needed for each fund.
records.frequency: rolling basis. The process of identifying grantees is unclear but could involve an expression of interest by interested groups.
records.targetGroups: Community Fisheries organizations · SMEs, women
records.requirements:
Eligibility criteria:
• The CFi must be fully registered and acknowledged by the Cambodian Fisheries Administration (FiA);
• The CFi must have a current:
o Signed agreement between the CFi and FiA establishing the legal authority of the CFI to manage their designated area
o Management plan
o By-laws
o Regulations
o Bank account
• The CFi must have an elected Community Fishery Committee (CFC) that:
o  is formally structured and active
o is officially approved by the relevant local authorities and fisheries administration.
• The CFi should have undertaken financial management training and demonstrated their ability to transparently and accountably manage funds.
• Each conservation trust fund is managed by a three-member Fund Committee, selected from the CFC. If none of these three members are women, then a fourth woman committee member has to be appointed from the
members of the CFC, or one or more woman members have to recruited at the next CFC elections to enable future representation.

CI Grants are deposited in the bank as interest-generating deposits. The CFi will need to open a term deposit for the principle, and if they don’t already have one, a saving account to receive the interest. This requires:
• An official letter from the commune chief which authorizes three members of the CFi Conservation Trust Fund Committee to represent the CFi and open a bank account;
• An official letter of acknowledgement from FiA;
• Copies of the latest CFi management plan, bylaws, regulations, and a signed CFi/FiA agreement establishing the CFi’s legal status;
• An official document detailing the CFC structure authorized by the Commune Chief;
• A document showing the official Commune Chief stamp that will be used to authorize any future banking transactions.
Two of the three authorized members of the Fund Committee (made up of CFC members) must act as joint signatories on the account, along with a Commune stamp.

The CFi becomes the owner of the conservation trust fund once the principal has been deposited in the term deposit account. When the term expires the CFi is required to reinvest the funds in another term deposit.

The CFi committee must apply for a grant from the Women’s Savings Group to access the interest generated by the Conservation Fund.  Before receiving a grant from the Women’s Savings Group generated by the Conservation Fund, the CFi committee must also:
• Have been trained in meeting procedures, committee management, Fisheries Law, gender in NRM, environmental protection, proposal and report writing, budget management, and SMART patrolling;
• Be engaged with their local Women’s Savings Group;
• Understand and be willing to adhere to the terms of Conservation Fund Grant agreements reached with the Women’s Savings Group, which may require gender sensitization training.

For more details, see Attachment 1 containing the Community fishery trust fund special terms and conditions in the linked protocol (Conservation International, February 2025) and the entry on Womens' Saving Group Conservation Funds.
records.whoCanApply: Community Fisheries organizations can access the funds subject to undergoing financial, organizational and gender-sensitive capacity-building and satisfying the eligibility criteria, the fulfilment of which CI provides support with.
records.enablingEnv:
Underlying programmes, policies and enabling institutions: As described in the Trust Fund setup protocol, the Commune Chief and Fisheries Administration Cantonment (provincial level of the FiA) play an important role in conservation trust fund management as they oversee the transparent operation of the fund and provide high level support to the Fund Committee. Therefore, proper registration and acknowledgement with authorities, as well as a trusting relationship with officials is essential.

Applicants: As described in the eligibility criteria, the CFi must be fully registered and acknowledged by the Cambodian Fisheries Administration and have a signed agreement assigning legal authority to manage their designated area, and have an elected, formally structured and officially approved Community Fishery Committee.

Standards applicable to institutions involved: The local governments are responsible for ensuring the CFis adhere to local, national and international laws and standards.
records.notes: See entry on CI Women's Savings Groups. Contact details: Phone: +855 23 238 627, Email: info-cicambodia@conservation.org. There is also the potential to obtain USD 1500 grants for "Revegetation Funds" though these are not separately elucidated in CI literature. The target activities include raising and replanting flooded forest seedlings; direct seeding of flooded forest tree species; and management of flooded forest areas under restoration.

records.name: Conservation International Community Based Fire Management Fund scheme
records.summary: CI helps Cambodian fishing communities on the Tonle Sap lake set up finance schemes to manage wildfire by providing them with basic fire suppression equipment, to help improve their livelihoods, health, security, and biodiversity conservation.
records.intermediaries: The funds are managed by the recipient organizations, which include CFIs and WSGs, with the help of local banks.
records.capital: Blended. Initial grants are made from CI funds which constitute a mix of public, private and philanthropic donors.
records.instruments: Grant, which is loaned out to members to support their small business activities and generated interest. This is done by integrating Women’s Saving Group’s into the Community Wildfire Management Team and providing them with a Community Based Fire Management Grant. · Grants
records.thematic: sustainable fisheries
records.size: USD 1000
records.frequency: rolling basis. The process of identifying grantees is unclear but could involve an expression of interest by interested groups.
records.targetGroups: Community Fishery Organizations (CFi’s), Community Protected Area Organizations (CPAs), and Villages · CSOs, local communities, women
records.activities:
Specific target activities include:
- Developing CFi fire management workplans;
- Community education sessions related to wildfire management; and
- Activities that assist the CFi in preventing and suppressing wildfire, within and adjacent to the CFi area.
records.requirements:
CI has not yet formalized the setup protocol for fire management funds and has hence not developed eligibility criteria. However, it emphasizes aspects crucual for success such as the following:
- The community should have adequate land tenure.
- To engage a village in combating forest fire, it is important to include the head of commune, village chief, and other community leaders in the fire management group.
- The establishment of each Community Wildfire Management Team should be formalized at the Commune level through written documentation signed by the CFi Chief, Village Chief, Commune Head, and if fire management funds are being provided by the local Women’s Saving Group, the Women’s Saving Group Chief.
- A high level of administrative and financial management capacity both within the Saving Group and wildfire Management Team.
records.whoCanApply: Fishing communities can apply for setting up Funds for fire management, though it is recommended that this is in conjunction with other formal community organizations like CFis and WSGs.
records.enablingEnv:
Underlying programmes, policies and enabling institutions:
- As described in the Trust Fund setup guide, the Commune Chief, Village Chief and other local authorities and community and religious leaders, especially pertaining to fisheries, can play an important role in fire management and should be integrated into the fire management team.
- The administration also plays an important role in recognizing and overseeing formal organizations like CFis, WSGs and Community Protected Areas (CPA’s), and in defining land tenure and use rights.
      - For example, the Cambodian Ministry of Environment has the authority to allocate sustainable use zones to communities residing within or adjacent to a protected area as a CPA, and approves the CPA management plan).
     - The establishment of each Community Wildfire Management Team is formalized at the Commune level through written documentation signed by the CFi Chief, Village Chief, Commune Head and if fire management funds are being provided by the local Women’s Saving Group, the Women’s Saving Group Chief.

Applicants:
- The community should have adequate land tenure.
- Engaging a formal community organization with a recognized structure to undertake fire management is recommended due to advantages like recognized community leadership, management capacity, financial resources such as bank accounts, and recognition by local authorities.

records.name: Ibis Rice Conservation Co., Ltd./Certified Wildlife Friendly certification
records.summary: The Wildlife Conservation Society Cambodia (WCS) has been supporting and promoting Ibis Rice™ for several years. Buyers (mainly up- market hotels and restaurants) pay a premium for "Certified Wildlife Friendly" products. Communities receive a share of the profits and assistance to move up the value chain so that farmers capture a greater proportion of the revenue and have an incentive to restrict farm expansion.
records.intermediaries: Target buyers include domestic tourist hotels and restaurants, food retailers and potentially international markets. The program has received certification from the Wildlife Friendly Enterprise Network.
records.implementers: The program was established by the Wildlife Conservation Society Cambodia (WCS) and is now managed under the Ibis Rice Conservation Co., Ltd., whose team in Cambodia handles all stages including purchasing raw rice directly from farmers under guaranteed contracts, rice processing, and final packaging.
records.capital: Private. The project has received funding from various sources. Currently it runs in the form of an incorporated company with a conservation-focused business model.
records.instruments: cooperative marketing label and benefit-sharing based business model · Other
records.thematic: biodiversity conservation, sustainable agriculture, climate change mitigation and adaptation, reducing deforestation
records.size: not applicable
records.frequency: Partner farmers and village marketing networks may be selected through an internal process.
records.targetGroups: paddy farmers · smallholders
records.activities: Ibis Rice buys paddy at a premium from village marketing networks, whose members are made up of farmers who are often not food secure and rely on forest resources for income. Communities receive a share of the profits and assistance to move up the value chain (e.g. through training in value-added processing, assistance with capital investment, and access to necessary micro loans). In addition to product sales, villagers are able to benefit from ecotourism and conserve the environment of Tonle Sap. Organic seeds and training on soil fertility, planting cover crops, rice seed preparation, and organic farming are also provided to farmers.
records.requirements: The process of farmers joining the Ibis Rice network is unclear.
records.enablingEnv:
Underlying programmes, policies and enabling institutions: Project records reveal that the provincial Department of Environment helped develop and implement zonation plans for wildlife sanctuaries around which paddy farming takes place, necessary for the certification programme to work. The Department of Land helps with monitoring rice fields.

Applicants: Mapping and registration of farming land has been an essential prerequisite for participation in the certification scheme.

Standards applicable: Farmers commit to organic farming as per US Department of Agriculture and EU standards, as well as zero deforestation and zero poaching, and adhere to requirements under the Certified Wildlife Friendly standard.

records.activities:
Grants support key design and implementation activities like legal and financial structuring, pipeline development, fundraising, piloting, and setting up impact measurement frameworks. They may explore the feasibility of a new solution and validate its potential (feasibility study) or support the design and structuring activities required to prepare for the vehicle’s possible launch (proof-of-concept).
Acceleration support includes:
- Ongoing technical feedback and guidance to refine investment models and strategies.
- Opportunities to connect with Convergence’s network of investors and ecosystem partners to expand partnerships and mobilize resources for climate action.
- Access to Convergence’s member trainings, blended finance data, market insights, and peer-learning opportunities.
records.requirements:
Eligibility criteria concern the following aspects:
Purpose:
- Proposals must articulate a clear need for grant support for the design and/or launch of an innovative blended finance vehicle.
- Solutions must target climate mitigation and/or adaptation.
- The proposed solution should be a financial instrument with a blended finance structure. It can be in the form of a fund, project finance vehicle, private company, bond, results-based financing, facility, or any other type of financial instrument.
- Vehicle must demonstrate potential to drive private investment at scale for development impact in Asia-Pacific.

Applicant types:
Proposals will only be accepted from organizations or consortium of organizations. For example, eligible organizations could include asset owners, asset managers, advisory firms, foundations, not-for-profit organizations, and private enterprises. The lead organization must be able to provide 1) proof of incorporation, and 2) financial statements for the previous fiscal year.

Focus geography:
Proposals target one or more developing market(s) in Asia. Applicants do not need to be domiciled in a developing market(s) but end beneficiaries and target activities must.

Evaluation criteria include:

1. Development Impact: inclusive, measurable and significant environmental and social impact; integration of impact across the design and implementation of the solution; Clear KPIs and use of global standards for measurement and monitoring of impact.

2. Track Record and Capabilities: experience in designing and managing investment vehicles; local presence and partnerships in target markets.

3. Additionality: Clear market gap and rationale for using a blended finance structuring approach; Potential to drive capital in targeted markets and create new investable opportunities; Strategic use of acceleration support and catalytic grant funding to scale.

4. Scalability and/or replicability: Clear capital structure and fundraising strategy; Potential to mobilize private capital at scale; Pathway to scale-up, reach target size, and replicate across markets.

5. Innovation & Demonstration Effect

6. Likelihood to achieve financial close: Bankability of the structure and alignment with investors’ risk–return profiles; Progress toward reaching a close and clarity on next steps; Robust risk management and governance framework.

7. Stakeholder Support: Support from key internal and external partners in the target region/country; Well-defined roles and engagement strategy for launch.
records.whoCanApply: Organizations of any kind with proof of incorporation may apply, which could include farmer and producer orginazations.
records.enablingEnv:
Enabling policies and programmes: One of the evaluation criteria concerns existing support from key internal and external partners in the target region/country.

Applicant requirements: Proof of incorporation required.

records.name: Cambodia's Article 6 Operational Manual
records.summary: In 2024, the Ministry of Environment, with the endorsement of the Cambodian Royal Government, approved the Operations Manual for the Implementation of Article 6 of the Paris Agreement on Climate Change in Cambodia. The Article 6 Operations Manual provides a detailed framework for issuing and transferring of Internationally Transferred Mitigation Outcomes (ITMOs), which are referred to as authorized Greenhouse Gas Emission Reductions (GHG ERs) in the Manual.
records.entityType: Other; market-based instrument; national government programme
records.intermediaries: The Government of Cambodia has designated the Ministry of Environment as the permanent National Authority for GHG ER Mechanisms, thus being the sole authorized entity to act on behalf of the government when issuing letters of no objection for GHG ER projects, and issuing letters of authorization and examination for GHG ERs generated from eligible projects in Cambodia.
records.capital: Blended, depending on participants in the mechanism.
records.thematic: climate change mitigation and adaptation, poverty allievation, sustainable agriculture/agroecology, ecosystem integrity, forest protection
records.size:
Authorizations for the international transfer of GHG ERs will be granted for a maximum period of either:
- 5 years, renewable a maximum of twice, for a total of 15 years; or
- 10 years with no option of renewal; or
- 15 years, renewable a maximum of twice, for a total of 45 years (only applicable for GHG ER projects involving removals)
records.frequency: Not applicable.
records.targetGroups: Local communiites, particularly poor and disadvantaged groups · local communities
records.activities:
The eligibility criteria for Article 6 authorization mention that target activities must be included in the ‘positive list’ of mitigation activities (i.e. activities in the Cambodian NDC designated as conditional upon international support. Key examples of such activities from the agriculture and forestry sector from Cambodia's NDC 3.0 July 2025 include:
- Increase the adoption of management and intermittent flooding in rice fields,
- Increase Mechanized Direct Seeded- Rice (mDSR),
- Enhance rice straw management practices,
- Introduce agroecological practices, land productivities including reducing tillage and sustainable agriculture (such as mulching, cover cropping, crop rotations, etc)
- Improve animal waste management for soil improvement and rural energy
- Improve fodder and feeding for livestock production
- Improve Good Agricultural Practices (GAP) and Sustainable Natural Rubber (SNR)
- Introduce agroforestry practices on rubber-high value timber for smallholders
- Introduce sustainable rubber wood harvesting
- Reduce deforestation through REDD+ Mechanism and other measures
- Transitioning to Certified and Sustainable Wood Energy and Feedstock
- Expand forest cover through afforestation and reforestation activities
- Increase forest carbon stocks through assisted natural regeneration (ANR) and other forest restoration measures
- Incorporate good and/or improved forest management practices to enhance forest carbon stocks as well as ecosystem integrity
- Introduce and promote agroforestry.
Further, activities must be aligned with Cambodia's sustainable development priorities which are divided into three main categories, i.e. “social enhancement of income and quality of life,” “technology transfer,” and “economic benefits”, and include:
  - Poverty alleviation,
  - Provision of community infrastructure,
  - Stakeholder consultation,
  - Access to community assets,
  - Equity in accessing the community benefits of the project for the target communities
  - Creation of employment
  - Public health
  - Gender equity
  - Adaptation
  - Transfer of appropriate and best available technology
  - Capacity building
  - Use of local businesses and industries
  - Share of project budget spent in country
  - Reduced dependence on fossil fuels and imported energy

Eligibility criteria for Article 6 authorization pertain to projects, not project proponents. They include:
- included in  ‘positive list’ of mitigation activities (i.e. activities in the updated NDC designated as conditional upon international support, as mentioned in the Target Activity column)
- partly reserved for domestic use.
- must be issued by an eligible carbon mechanism (bilateral, e.g. Joint Crediting Mechanism; independent, e.g. Gold Standard and Verified Carbon Standard; Art. 6.4)

The application process includes obtaining a no objection certificate from the national authority for GHG ER mechanisms, followed by validation of prject design by an independent auditor, letter of authorization by the national authority

Underlying policies and programmes: The Manual is a key financing mechanism to implement Cambodia's commitments under its NDC for the UNFCCC Paris Agreement, especially with regard to mitigation activities designated as conditional upon international support in its NDC. Its success requires the development of the technical capacity of entities such as the Ministry of Environment to discharge its role as the National Authority that monitors compliance with the Operational Manual's processes.
Standards applicable: The ER must be issued by an eligible carbon mechanism (bilateral, e.g. Joint Crediting Mechanism; independent, e.g. Gold Standard and Verified Carbon Standard; Art. 6.4).

Access is driven by the strength of national climate strategies (e.g., NDCs, NAPs), sectoral alignment, and institutional readiness to implement large-scale investments. Projects are expected to deliver measurable mitigation or adaptation benefits, demonstrate financial soundness, and show clear potential for scalability and transformational impact.

records.name: GCF Local Governments and Climate Change Phase 3 (LGCC-3)/ Local Climate Adaptive Living Facility (LoCAL)/Performance-Based Climate Resilience Grant (PBCRG) Facility
records.summary:
This programme is the third (scale-up) phase of the Local Governments and Climate Change initiative, part of the Local Climate Adaptive Living Facility (LoCAL)/Performance-Based Climate Resilience Grant (PBCRG) Facility in Cambodia. It is implemented through the National Committee for Sub-National Democratic Development (NCDD) and allows district administrations to draw direct grants based on verified climate-responsive performance. The project’s main objective is to integrate climate change adaptation into local development planning and finance. This is the first time Cambodia has accessed GCF financing through a direct accredited entity. The project will be rolled out over three years and initially focus on 15 districts across Battambang, Preah Vihear and Pursat provinces, with an additional ten districts to be added in the final year. The programme was initially launched in 2011 with the help of the UN Capital Development Fund.

PBCRGs are performance-based grants that provide a financial top-up to cover the additional costs of making investments climate resilient. They complement regular allocations made by the central level to local governments through the intergovernmental fiscal transfer system. A key feature of LGCC-3 will be to create allocations for climate change adaption in the regular investment budgets of the local governments i.e. districts, municipalities, and khans (urban districts).
records.intermediaries:
The National Committee for Sub-National Democratic Development (NCDD) is the accredited Direct Access Entity for the GCF in Cambodia, and will act as the Executing Entity for the project. Local governments recieving the grants will plan, budget, and implement climate-resilient investments addressing their most pressing adaptation needs,  in close consultation with communities. In the past, the modality has been supported by a
range of donors and projects, including LGCC-I and II, ASPIRE, SRELFOOD, and SRL.
records.capital: Public.
records.thematic: Climate change adaptation, sustainable agriculture, health, water, infrastructure
records.size:
On average, each local government will receive approximately USD 60,000 per year.

The project comprises a USD 9.8 million grant from the GCF and co-financed grant of USD 216,000. Of this, USD 5.4 million will be channelled through around 90 sub-grants to local governments through the PBCRG Facility. The implementation period is around 5 years, 2026 - 2031.
records.frequency: Funds will be disbursed in line with annual local planning and budget cycles. The programme implementation is based on LoCAL’s system of Performance-Based Climate Resilience Grants (PBCRGs) which uses existing governmental fiscal transfer systems and includes incentives for Local Governments based on annual performance assessments.
records.targetGroups: District governments, local communities · governments, local communities
records.activities:
The programme supports local governments in developing climate-resilient rural infrastructure and adaptation measures in key sectors including climate-resilient and diversified livelihood options, targeting the most vulnerable people and communities, health and wellbeing, food and water security, infrastructure and built environment, and ecosystem preservation and restoration. LGCC-3 will be implemented in 25 districts that are particularly vulnerable to the impacts of climate change, such as climate-induced floods and droughts. The following climate-sensitive sectors will be  targeted:
- Community-based Natural Resource Management
- Agriculture and Food security
- Water Resources Management
- Rehabilitate of public facilities and infrastructure for resilience
- Human Health
records.requirements:
All proposed adaptation interventions and related activities will undergo mandatory Environmental and Social Safeguard (ESS) screening following the procedure set by the implementing authority, and its Environmental and Social Action Plan, before being selected for direct funding from the PBCRG facility. Districts are free to use the grant to finance activities from the menu of eligible activities (Section 4.2 of Annex 13 Operations Manual) that have a clear and direct link with the adaptation priorities identified by the district administration following public consultation.

The following "minimum conditions" need to be satisfied for districts to be eligible for funding:
First cycle:
- The district has an annual prioritised and costed plan of climate change action plan for climate change adaptation activities, that has taken into account the:
(i) Vulnerability Risk Assessment (VRA);
(ii) the vision of the Enhanced District Climate Change Adaptation Strategy (EDCCAS), and
(iii) results of consultations with citizens

Additional conditions for second cycle:
- PBCRG-funds received in the current year are (i) used as per the Climate Change Action plan, (ii) for eligible activities; and (iii) implementation is on track and will (likely) be finished before the end of the financial year.
- The CCA projects foreseen under the District, Municipal, Khan (DMK) investment budget for the current year are (i) being implemented; (ii) qualify as Climate Change Adaptation as specified and (iii) will (likely) be finished before the end of the financial year.
- In the 12 months preceding the performance assessment, the district has, in a timely manner, complied with all the (to be specified) reporting requirements with regards to the use of the grant and the CCA activities financed from its own/other resources. Access to, and the size of, the grant therefore depends on the performance assessment.

Overall, Participatory planning and budgeting are critical elements of the LGCC/LoCAL approach, and preparation and annual updating of the District Climate Change Adaptation Action Plan (DCCAAP) will be a participatory bottom-up process, supplemented by client science as well as the outcomes of the Vulnerability Risk Assessment. As part of the annual planning and budget process (including the updating of the DCCAAP) the districts are expected to organise consultations in communes.
records.enablingEnv:
Underlying programmes, policies and relevant institutions: As mentioned in project documents, LGCC-3 will focus on District local governments, which are seen as the lowest level for public sector service delivery. The  specific objective of the LoCAL under Phase III is to demonstrate that District Administrations are able and willing to visibly allocate part of their District, Municipal, Khan (DMK) investment fund for activities related to Climate Change Adaptation. The LGCC-PBCRG shall be aligned with the DMK allocations, and the grants be made available to the DMK administrations.

The LGCC approach will further align with the National Program on Sub-National Democratic Development, which is now in its second phase (2021-2030), amongst others, aiming to make the DMK Administrations the prime and principal level of decentralised sub national service delivery.

Applicant requirements: As detailed in the Requirements section, discrict governments must undertake participatory planning and budgeting to prepare the district climate change action plan and adaptation action plan in order to access funding.

Standards applicable: Planning has to be gender-sensitive and culturally appropriate. Proposed adaptation interventions will undergo mandatory Environmental and Social Safeguard (ESS) screening following the procedure set by the implementing authority, and its Environmental and Social Action Plan.

records.name: Mekong–Republic of Korea Cooperation Fund (MKCF)
records.summary: The Mekong–Republic of Korea Cooperation Fund (MKCF) is a regional funding mechanism under the Mekong–ROK cooperation framework. It supports regional collaboration, sustainable development, people-centered partnerships, and stronger cooperation between Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Vietnam, Thailand and South Korea. The fund is focused on projects that solve shared regional challenges and create long-term benefits across the Mekong subregion, including (but not limited to) those with a focus on agricultural and rural development and the environment.

records.thematic: Agriculture and rural development, environment, infrastructure, culture and tourism, human resources development, information and communication technology (ICT), non-traditional security challenges
records.size: USD 300,000 to USD 1,000,000 per project for 2-3 years
records.frequency: Once in 1-2 years, the MKCF is now in ist tenth cycle since establishment in 2013.

Projects must align with the Mekong–ROK Plan of Action priority sectors as mentioned in the Scope section. Cross-sectoral and integrated approaches are encouraged if they increase regional value and collaboration. For the 10th call, MKCF is prioritizing innovative regional initiatives that:
- Address shared development challenges
- Respond to cross-border or regional issues
- Strengthen Mekong–ROK cooperation
- Deliver clear and measurable results
- Show sustainable impact
- Demonstrate potential for scaling up and replication
- Clearly show regional relevance and benefits for both the Mekong subregion and the Republic of Korea.
records.requirements:
Eligible applicants include government agencies, autonomous organizations, academic institutions, training institutions, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), and international organizations, including UN agencies.

Applicants should be based in or connected to the Mekong region or South Korea. Whether based in one or more countries, the project should demonstrate regional impact.

Eligible institutions are invited to submit an Expression of Interest (EOI) that demonstrates eligibility, alignment with a priority sector, builds a regional case, demonstrates impact (through expected outcomes, measurable results, sustainability and replication or scale-up potential), and if possible, includes regional co-implementers, development partners, technical institutions, and South Korea–Mekong collaboration elements.  The fund encourages triangular partnerships, multi-partner collaboration, and engagement with other development partners.

Applicants must submit an Expression of Interest (EOI) in PDF format through the respective Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) of the five Mekong countries or the ROK.
records.whoCanApply: Farmer producer groups may be able to access these funds as NGOs.
records.enablingEnv: Underlying programmes: The Fund is a critical mechanism to facilitate the Mekong-Republic of Korea regional cooperation partnership established in 2011 through the Han River Declaration. As part of this commitment, the Government of the Republic of Korea pledged to expand its Official Development Assistance (ODA) to ASEAN Member States, with particular emphasis on supporting the development of the Mekong countries.
records.notes: The submission deadline for the latest call is April 10, 2026. Contact address: dutta@mekonginstitute.org

records.name: Least Developed Countries Fund (LDCF)
records.summary: The LDCF and SCFF are sister funds managed by the GEF to serve the Paris Agreement. The LDCF is the only facility exclusively dedicated to helping LDCs adapt to climate change. These channels support diverse activities including institutional strengthening, landscape restoration, and localized resilience-building. LDCF funding helps least developed countries address their short-, medium-, and long-term resilience needs and reduce climate change vulnerability in priority sectors and ecosystems.
records.intermediaries: The LDCF works through formally accredited GEF Agencies. Among them are UN agencies, multilateral and regional development banks, national government institutions, and international and non-governmental organisations.
records.capital: Public, based on voluntary contributions from developed country parties to the UNFCCC
records.thematic: Climate change adaptation, agriculture, disaster risk reduction, economic recovery, health, industry and infrastructure, oceans and coasts, waste
records.size: The total LDCF contribution for a Medium-Sized Project (MSP) cannot exceed USD 5 million. Beyond that, the project is considered a Full-Sized Project (FSP).
records.frequency: Project applications are typically initiated by member countries based on their priorities and requirements on a rolling basis.
records.targetGroups: Least developed countries · governments
records.activities:
The LDCF works with partner agencies to bolster technical and institutional capacity at the national and local level, to create a policy environment that encourages investment in adaptation solutions, to reduce systemic barriers to progress, and to promote innovation and private sector engagement.

LDCF funding has addressed a range of adaptation priorities in the LDCs across a range of vulnerable sectors including agriculture, water, disaster risk management, coastal zone management, infrastructure, and sustainable alternate livelihoods among others. The GEF-8 adaptation strategy for the LDCF/SCCF aims to focus on agriculture, food security and health, water, climate information services, and nature-based solutions. The strategy aims to further support LDCs in addressing their adaptation priorities by scaling up access to adaptation finance, strengthen innovation and private sector engagement, and foster whole-of-society approach and partnerships for inclusion.
records.requirements:
LDCF project criteria are based on UNFCCC COP guidance and include:
- Country ownership: projects must be nationally identified priorities with stakeholder consultation
- Programme and policy conformity: alignment with LDCF strategy and stakeholder involvement
- Financing: includes cost-effectiveness and co-financing considerations
- Institutional coordination and support
- Monitoring and evaluation
- To access funding, countries must work with one of the 18 accredited GEF Agencies, which submit proposals on their behalf. A project also requires endorsement by the country’s GEF Operational Focal Point.
- Enabling Activities – such as the preparation of NAPs or national climate reports—are eligible for support under the LDCF.
records.whoCanApply: Grants are accessible for national governments of least developed countries that are part of the UNFCCC.
records.notes: In 2024, the LDCF and SCCF approved more than USD 36 million towards boosting climate resilience and fostering inclusive, green economic development in Cambodia, Comoros, São Tomé and Principe, and Somalia. In Cambodia, the proposed project will improve the management of vulnerable landscapes and watersheds in the Tonle Sap Basin, with a focus on conserving and restoring forests, improving water resource management, and promoting sustainable livelihoods. The project will explore innovative finance mechanisms to scale the approach in the future.

records.name: Special Climate Change Fund (SCCF)
records.summary: The  SCFF and LDCF are sister funds managed by the GEF to serve the Paris Agreement and the climate adaptation efforts of developing countries. The SCCF  supports adaptation-focused technology transfer, innovation, and private sector engagement across all developing countries, apart from providing dedicated funding to support the climate adaptation needs of Small Island Developing States.
records.intermediaries: GEF Partners Agencies (GEF Agencies) are the only institutions that access GEF funding directly on behalf of an eligible recipient (government) for the design and implementation of GEF-financed projects. There are currently 18 GEF Agencies including UN agencies, multilateral development banks, international financial institutions, and NGOs. Projects can be executed on the ground by any organization, including private sector, civil society, government and non-governmental organizations.
records.capital: Public, based on voluntary contributions from developed country parties to the UNFCCC
records.thematic: Climate change adaptation, agriculture, disaster risk reduction, economic recovery, health, industry and infrastructure, jobs, nature based solutions and ecosystem services, oceans and coasts, waste, water, rural development
records.size: The total SCCF  contribution for a Medium-Sized Project (MSP) cannot exceed USD 5 million. Beyond that, the project is considered a Full-Sized Project (FSP). As of November 2024, the cumulative pledges to the Fund amount to approximately USD 460 million, with USD 422 million delivered to its trust fund.
records.frequency: Project applications are typically initiated by member countries based on their priorities and requirements on a rolling basis.
records.targetGroups: Non-annex 1 member countries UNFCCC · governments
records.activities: Activities funded by the SCCF have fostered improvements in agriculture, water resources, disaster risk management, infrastructure, climate information systems, natural resource and integrated coastal zone management, as well as climate change-driven disease prevention. SCCF financing has also bolstered the climate resilience of public infrastructure such as schools, roads, and ports, supported the development of catastrophe risk insurance, and supported small and medium-sized enterprises in the adaptation space.
records.requirements: Since the SCCF is administrated by the GEF, countries seeking SCCF funding work with a GEF Partner Agency to submit project proposals.  Projects must be driven by the country (rather than by an external partner) and be consistent with national priorities that support sustainable development. SCCF is mainly available to projects that are endorsed by governments in eligible countries.
records.whoCanApply: No

records.name: LOLC Cambodia
records.summary: LOLC Cambodia Plc. (LOLC) is a licensed microfinance deposit-taking institution (MDI) committed to serving customers at the bottom of the pyramid, founded in 1994 by Catholic Relief Services. With a nationwide presence of 81 branches across Cambodia, LOLC offers a range of credit, savings, leasing, and digital banking options with the vision that families at the base of the socio-economic pyramid are empowered to live their lives with dignity, social and economic security, and justice.
records.intermediaries: These include lending partners (see Capital Source), loan collection partners (e.g. Wing Bank), microinsurance partners (e.g. Serendib Microinsurance), technical assistance providers (e.g. Oiko Credit and Global Climate Partnership Fund), and guarantee partners (e.g. USAID and the Credit Guarantee Corporation of Cambodia).
records.capital: Blended, including private customer deposits, and lending partners such as Development Finance Institutions (DFIs), overseas banks, local banks, and overseas fund managers, e.g.  Abler Nordic (formerly the Norway Microfinance Initiative), alterfin, Blue Earth Capital, responsability, Norfund. LOLC (Cambodia) Plc. is co-owned by LOLC Asia Private Limited (based in Singapore) and TPC-ESOP Co, Ltd.
records.instruments: credit (including group and individual micro-loans, SME loans, seasonal loans designed to match crop cycles), savings, leasing, microinsurance, digital banking · Loans, insurance/de-risking products, other
records.thematic: economic resilience, sustainable livelihoods, women's empowerment
records.size:

SME loan: above KHR 40,000,00 or USD 10,000 for 3-120 months (short to long term)

records.activities: The Company’s products and services are designed to give their predominantly rural customers access to economic opportunities to both develop businesses and improve their quality of life.
records.requirements:
Seasonal Loan
- supports farmers and traders in agriculture activities such as animal raising, fishing, agri-business, and relevant agriculture productions.  This loan provides clients who have a reliable and stable source of income and strong collateral, but their income-based activities are on a seasonal basis rather than a steady monthly income.

eligibility:
Be a majority aged 18 to 65 years old
Permanent resident
Have a legal business and regular income
Have a good record and be reliable
Have enough capacity to repay the loan
Have ID card, passport, family book, resident book, and/or birth certificate

Small and Medium Enterprise Loan (SME)
- aims to support individuals, companies or enterprises in running or expanding their businesses in all legal sectors, including trade, services, agri-businesses and manufacturing. The loan product targets small to medium size businesses.

eligibility: same as above

Group Loan
- aims to help clients run and to grow their micro or small businesses. The target clients should have or operate a micro or small business and require funds for working capital or acquisition of fixed assets. Prospective clients are encouraged to form joint-liability groups of 2-7 members among their community members with similar needs. There is no requirement of physical collateral.

eligibility: same as above, with the following additional requirements:
- Create a joint-liability group ranging from 2 to 7 members per group with the selection of a group leader
- similar purpose in using the loan.
records.whoCanApply: The loan services mentioned previously are accessible for farmers and producers having a 'legal business' individually or as enterprises, particularly micro and small businesses, which should also include cooperatives and other producer organizations.
records.enablingEnv:
Underlying legal instruments: LOLC Cambodia functions in accordance with its microfinance institution licence and microfinance deposit-taking license from the National Bank of Cambodia.

Applicant requirements: In the loan product examples given previously, having a 'legal business' is stated as a requirement, but aspects regarding incorporation and registration are not explained. For group loans, the formation of a joint lliability group is required.

Standards applicable: LOLC Cambodia adheres to strict standards regarding the use of its financial services and was awarded the Stakeholder-Verified Orange Seal by IIX, recognising its strong commitment to gender equality and environmental sustainability.

For instance, its list of Prohibited Activities includes:
- Production or trade in any product or activity deemed illegal under host country laws or regulations or international conventions and agreements, including requirements related to environmental, health and safety and labour aspects.
- Fishing activity using a driftnet in excess of 2.5 km in length.
- Production or activities involving harmful or exploitative forms of forced labor/harmful child labor.
- Production or activities that impinge on the lands owned, or claimed under adjudication, by Indigenous Peoples, without full documented consent of such peoples.
- Plantation projects that would require the removal of existing non-degraded natural forest.
- Projects whose purpose and/or approach are inconsistent with human rights, and in the case of private sector financing, projects underpinned by rationales that clearly contradict the United Nations Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights.
